title: Scribe a full circle with spring dividers, keeping the point seated in the center-punch mark all the way round
instruction: Scribe the full circle for the hole on the blue steel plate with the dividers, centered on the punch mark, then stand the dividers back in the cork.
context: Most people have drawn a circle with a school compass and know the catch: the point has to stay in its hole while the other leg goes all the way round, and a hand that lets the pressure off or turns the wrist too far lets it slip and spoils the circle. Machinists and sheet-metal workers do the same in steel when they lay out a hole: they set one point of a pair of spring dividers in a center-punch mark, press lightly on the handle and swing the other leg a full turn so its point scribes the circle through the layout dye. If the point skates out mid-swing, the rest of the line comes out doubled or off-center, and a scribed line in steel can't be rubbed out. Starting off the mark gives a circle with the wrong center, and stopping short leaves a gap. Dividers stand on two points in a line, so they can't be let go on the plate partway round. They go back in their cork so the points stay sharp.
setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, with x forward, y to the robot's left and the table top at z 0; the layout is the same in every trial. A mild steel plate, 13 x 11.5 cm and 6 mm thick, coated with blue layout dye, lies fixed on the table at x 20 to 33, y -15.5 to -4. Two bright scribed center lines, 9 cm long, cross on it at x 26, y -10, where there is a center-punch mark about 2 mm across: the center of a 60 mm hole to lay out. A dark cork block, 6 x 6 cm and 6 mm thick (its top level with the plate's), is fixed at x 23 to 29, y -24.5 to -18.5, 3 cm to the robot's right of the plate. A pair of 100 mm spring dividers (80 g), already set to a 30 mm radius, stands upright with both points stuck in the cork, its legs along x (points at x 24.5 and 27.5, y -21.5). The two steel legs meet a spring bow 9.6 cm up, with an adjusting screw and nut across them; on top is a black knurled handle 2.6 cm across and 2.4 cm tall (11.2 to 13.6 cm above the points, 20 g), centered between the legs, a sleeve that turns freely on its stem and slides 4 mm down it against a light spring (1.5 N at rest, 3.5 N fully down). The dividers can be lifted, carried and turned, and drop back onto the steel or cork under their own weight. They stand on their own only with their points stuck in the cork; let go standing on the steel, they tip over onto their side. Nothing else is on the table.
scoring: The scorer watches the whole run. The points are down when within 0.5 mm of the steel. The pivot point is seated in the punch mark when the points are down and it drops within 0.5 mm of the mark's center (a lightly struck mark is about 2 mm across with a 90-degree cone); it stays seated until pushed 1.5 mm off (the mark's 1 mm rim plus 0.5 mm for the sim's play in the seated point), or until the dividers have turned 1 degree (0.5 mm at the scribing point, about the mark's depth) away from where the handle stopped being pressed at least 1.5 mm (2.25 N, a light fingertip press): unpressed, the scribing point's drag lifts the pivot out. The arc is the set of 0.1-degree sectors of the circle the scribing leg swept with the pivot seated (back and forth over the same sector counts once). Score 0, irreversibly, if either point ever moved more than 1 mm in all over the plate while down without the pivot seated: starting off the mark, skating out of it mid-swing, or dragging the dividers across the plate (a stray scratch that long shows plainly in layout dye and reads as a second line). Dividers stand on two points in a line, so let go with the points on the plate they fall over and the pivot point leaves the mark: once no hand has held the handle (the gripper's own shape touching it, to a 2 mm contact tolerance, with the fingers stopped by it, not an empty fist or open hand) for 2 steps in a row with the points on the plate, or they lean more than 10 degrees there, nothing scribed after counts. Nothing counts while a hand still touches the dividers: the job ends with them let go. Otherwise, at the end: 1.0 with at least 355 degrees scribed (a 5-degree gap is 2.6 mm on the 60 mm circle, about a saw kerf) and the dividers standing back in the cork (points down, both at least 3 mm inside its edges) and let go; 0.75 at least 355 degrees scribed with the dividers left elsewhere; 0.5 at least 180 degrees scribed (half the circle, the least that is real progress); 0 otherwise, including doing nothing. Possible scores: 0, 0.5, 0.75 and 1.0. In a real trial the handle's press is not measured, since the line shows whether the point stayed in the mark: film from above (a fall shows on it), then check the plate under a loupe for one clean circle with no doubled or offset arc or scratch, its radius from the punch mark checked with a scale at eight places round it, the gap measured with the scale, and the dividers standing in the cork.
reset_notes: Stand the dividers back in the cork block, the handle over its center and the legs along x, set to a 30 mm radius. A scribed line can't be removed: use a fresh plate (or re-dye this one, scribe the center lines and punch the mark at the same place).
fidelity: The dividers are rigid, spread fixed at 30 mm, and tip only about the line of their points; carried, the grip holds them upright, as a hand does. The handle is enlarged from about 8 mm to 2.6 cm. A punch mark captures a lightly pressed point (that is what it is for); the sim's seat, which holds the slides to 0.3 mm while pressed in, stands in for that, and a real trial checks the circle is concentric with the mark. The line is drawn as 1.6 mm dots; point friction is damping.
